title: Instant Dukkha, Suzuki Roshi Walk Like an Elephant
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up Shunryu Suzuki's "Walk Like an Elephant," a 1970 talk collected in Not Always So, and reads two passages from it about practicing zazen step by step without a gaining idea. Kanho begins with instant suffering in the 21st century, from Kindle pre-orders to the damage Instagram bullying does to young people. A Russian doll set stands for the lineage running from Suzuki through Uchiyama, Dogen, and Bodhidharma back to the Buddha. Kanho then returns to last Sunday's "worry box," describing how opening it on the cushion becomes an invitation to the suffering to visit, and closes with Mary Oliver's poem "Heavy."

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good evening.
I hope that you, your families, and your loved ones are doing well and that there is ease.

At the same time I realized that while my wish for your health and happiness and well-being and the health and happiness of your loved ones is sincere, probably we and they are all suffering to a certain degree.
Sometimes it is subtle, sometimes intense, and sometimes it feels like our heart is breaking.
This is the nature of being alive.
This is the truth the Buddha recognized and taught as the first noble truth.
In the 21st century, we created some new ways of suffering for ourselves and others.
One advantage is that nowadays we can do almost everything so much faster, including the creation of suffering.
Instantly, we can be almost anywhere, check out anything, travel through images and movies and videos anywhere in this world.
For example, I can hear about a book, read reviews about it, download it and start reading within maybe five minutes or less.
I can even pre-order a book that is not yet published, and as soon as the book is released, it shows up on my Kindle.
You may ask, how is the suffering?
I confess that I love to read, and therefore this particular item is not so much in the dukkha category.
On the other hand, I have a whole stack of books that I'm trying to read and study.
So maybe a little bit of dukkha is hiding in there.
But the same principle of instantaneous satisfaction or dissatisfaction hides everywhere.
This past week, it was reported how damaging the use of social media can be to young people.
Simply growing up and being a teenager is already really tough: expectations from parents, trying to figure out what life is all about.
The competition and the put-downs by peers create a lot of anguish.
School and social life create lots of pressure.
It used to be, at least in those ancient times while I was growing up, that one only had to deal with a limited group, depending on where I was and what I was doing.
However, through social media, like WhatsApp and Instagram, and let's face it, Facebook is something for old folks like me.
There is no break, no reprieve from this pressure.

Parents and child development experts find that this nonstop comparison and bullying is very harmful to the self-esteem, confidence and overall mental health of young people, especially girls and women.
They feel as if their bodies aren't good enough, as people add filters and edit their pictures in order for them to look perfect.
Plastic-looking people, Barbie lookalikes, all the humanity stripped from faces seems to be what they call perfect.
Bullying on Instagram has led users to commit suicide and to attempt suicide and to cause self-harm.
It has caused depressive episodes and anxiety.
In this accelerated world, we Zen practitioners choose to step away from the doom-scrolling to sit down and do nothing.
And it's not the same as doing nothing like eating cookies while watching the latest movie just released on Netflix.
We choose to do zazen, and through that we are choosing to slow down our life.
So Tim asked me to talk a bit about Shunryu Suzuki tonight.
There is a collection of informal talks published as the book *Not Always So*, which is my favorite.
I know *Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind* is the very famous book, but *Not Always So* contains quite a few talks that I absolutely loved.
One of the talks is titled "Walk Like an Elephant."
A brief side note: you can actually find an audio recording of the talk.
It's under SuzukiRoshi.EngageWisdom.com, Talks, Walk, Elephant and Sitting Like a Frog.
If you're interested, please just shoot me an email.
I'll be happy to email you the link.
Or maybe we can post it with the talk.
Tonight, I would like to read you two sections from this talk.
The first one is at the very beginning.
*Walk like an elephant.
All the teachings come from practicing zazen, where Buddha's mind is transmitted to us.
To sit is to open up our transmitted mind and all the treasures we experience come from this mind.
To realize our true mind or transmitted mind, we practice zazen.
Many people seek for a special place and become confused.
As Dogen Zenji says, "Why give up your own seat and wander about in the dusty realms of foreign countries?"*
*When we are sightseeing, we are involved in an idea of hasty attainment.
Our way is to go step by step, appreciating our everyday life.
Then we can see what we are doing, where we are.
People often think it would be best to study Zen in Japan, but this is rather difficult.
"Why don't you stay at Zen Center?"
I ask them.
If you go to Japan, mostly you will encourage them to build more new buildings, like hotels.
They may be very happy to see you, but it is a waste of time and money, and you will be discouraged because you cannot find a good Zen master.*
*And even if you find a teacher, it will be difficult to understand him and to study with him.
You can do true zazen practice here, watching yourself step by step, one step after another.
We practice like a cow rather than a horse.
Instead of galloping about, we walk slowly like a cow or an elephant.
If you can walk slowly without any idea of gain, then you are already a good Zen student.*
I don't know about cows being slow.
I got chased by a water buffalo once, and I barely got away.
So I'm not so sure about slow cows.
This talk by Shunryu Suzuki was almost given in a different age, in a different time.
It was 50 years ago, in August of 1970.
I felt that it touched on the same subject of accelerated time.
Writing this talk, reading up for it and studying for it, I felt like part of a Russian doll set.
You know those dolls: every time you peel off a layer, there's another doll hidden inside, and you think you're done and there's another one and another one.
So I am writing this talk, and I'm reading a book of talks by Shunryu Suzuki, first doll, and I heard of him through my teachers.
And Shunryu Suzuki in his talk, which was given at Zen Center, quotes Uchiyama Roshi, Bodhidharma, and Dogen, more dolls.
And we know today that Dogen's writing references and relies heavily on Chinese writing and the Chinese Zen tradition.
Zen was brought to China from India by Bodhidharma.
And of course, all these teachers and all these teachings are rooted in the Buddha and his teachings.
This is what it means to be part of a living tradition, mind to mind, warm hand to warm hand.
Maybe today warm screen to warm screen.
This is the statement which is usually ascribed to Bodhidharma.
*A special transmission outside the scriptures, no dependency on words and letters, pointing directly to the human mind, seeing into one's nature and attaining Buddhahood.*
Back to "Walk Like an Elephant."
Suzuki Roshi is talking about this mindset, this belief that if we were somewhere else, we would definitely find something better and more true.
Walking like an elephant is important.
The point is not so much a rush to get to the destination, but rather the unstoppable force of the elephant.
And can you imagine a herd of elephants?
A force of nature.
Or maybe we should take up the other practice of practicing like a cow.
What would that look like?
I am sure if you are a cow, harassment on Instagram is not an issue.
Of course, as a cow, one would have a different set of problems.
Now the second quote from "Walk Like an Elephant," which addresses the practice of zazen without having a gaining idea, without having any idea of fame and profit.
*When we practice zazen, we are practicing with all the ancestors.
You should clearly know this point.
You cannot waste your time even though your zazen is not so good.
You may not even understand what it is, but someday, sometime, someone will accept your practice.
So just practice without wandering, without being involved in sightseeing zazen.
Then you have a chance to join our practice.
Good or bad does not matter.
If you sit with this understanding, having conviction in your Buddha nature, then sooner or later you will find yourself in the midst of great Zen masters.
So the important point is to practice without any idea of a hasty gain, without any idea of fame or profit.
Do not practice zazen for the sake of others or for the sake of ourselves.
Just practice zazen for the sake of zazen.
Just sit.*
Thank you very much.
So that was the ending of that talk, "Walk Like an Elephant."
I would like, however, to expand a little on Suzuki Roshi's mention of gaining idea.
And please forgive me if I loop back to last Sunday's talk.
I talked about my worry box, my invisible but rather large box full of worries, concerns, anxieties that I carry with me.
It's invisible and yet quite the burden.
I talked about the fact that sometimes I intentionally take my worry box to the cushion.
I mentioned that, in fact, every once in a while I need to take my worry box with me.
I know how to sit until the time is right, and then I gently open the box.
I carefully take out some worries, some conditioning, some pain, and I sit with it on the cushion.
It seems that only there I can see it for what it is.
In the follow-up conversation after the talk, someone mentioned the idea that in zazen we should almost be removed from those troubles and pains.
I am bringing this up again, and maybe you ask why.
To me, our Zen practice is very pragmatic, very useful.
It can help us resolve old karma.
It can help us understand our pain, where it is coming from, and how we carry it.
To me, this does not fall under a gaining idea.
I don't say, well, tonight I'll figure out this problem or tonight I'll finally fix myself.
It's not like this.
It is an offering to my suffering.
It is an invitation to the suffering to come visit.
It's an invitation to share time.
I allow myself to feel the weight of the pain and to be curious.
I am curious about what it feels like, how it started, how I carry it, why I carry it.
We become intimate.
I would like to end tonight's talk with Mary Oliver's poem, "Heavy."
*That time I thought I could not go any closer to grief without dying, I went closer, and I did not die.
Surely God had his hand in this, as well as friends.
Still I was bent, and my laughter, as the poet said, was nowhere to be found.
Then said my friend Daniel, brave even among lions, "It's not the weight you carry, but how you carry it, books, bricks, grief.
It's all in the way you embrace it, balance it, carry it, when you cannot or would not put it down."*
*So I went practicing.
Have you noticed?
Have you heard the laughter that comes now and again out of my startled mouth?
How I linger to admire, admire, admire the things of this world that are kind and maybe also troubled: roses in the wind, the sea geese on the steep waves, a love to which there is no reply.*
If you found something useful in tonight's talk, I am glad.
If you did not, please continue with your practice without being disturbed by my words.
Thank you very much.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
